standard.title: Similarities and differences between places in Australia and neighbouring countries
standard.description: the similarities and differences between places in Australia and neighbouring countries in terms of their natural, managed and constructed features
standard.prior_knowledge: From Y1 (AC9HS1K03): Students classified local place features as natural, managed and constructed. From Y2 (AC9HS2K03): Students explored geographical scales from local to state/territory.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify and describe similarities and differences between places in Australia and neighbouring countries in terms of natural, managed and constructed features.

nodes.label: Climatic types and natural features
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the main climatic types in Australia and neighbouring countries and describe the natural features associated with each.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two climatic types and describe one natural feature associated with each.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and locate examples of equatorial, tropical, arid, semi-arid and temperate climatic types in Australia and neighbouring countries; describe features of each climate type and their impact on other natural features.
wider: Compare how climate affects the natural features of a place in Australia with those in a contrasting country (e.g. Indonesia or a Pacific Island nation)
Investigate how animals and plants have adapted to specific climatic conditions in Australia and a neighbouring country
nodes.hinge_reason: Climate is the primary driver of natural feature variation — without climate knowledge, comparisons of natural features lack explanatory power.

response_modes.reason: The relationship between climate and natural features is causal — model the connection explicitly before expecting students to apply it in comparisons.

success_criteria: Names at least two climatic types
Describes one natural feature associated with each climatic type

nodes.label: Comparing Australia with a neighbouring country
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare Australia with at least one neighbouring country in terms of natural, managed and constructed features, identifying similarities and differences.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare at least two features (natural, managed or constructed) between Australia and one neighbouring country, identifying one similarity and one difference.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and describe similarities and differences in natural features (rocks, landforms, water bodies, climate, vegetation, animal life) and in housing, settlement types and built/managed environments between Australia and a neighbouring country.
wider: Compare settlement patterns and classify them into hierarchical categories (isolated dwellings to large cities) for both Australia and a neighbouring country
Investigate why similar natural environments in different countries have been developed differently by their inhabitants

response_modes.reason: Comparing across multiple feature categories (natural, managed, constructed) gives richer comparison than focusing on one type.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Comparison across natural and human-made features reveals how environment shapes human responses — students who compare only natural features miss the managed/constructed layer of analysis.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one similarity and one difference between Australia and a neighbouring country
Comparison covers at least two feature types (natural, managed or constructed)
